A cardiac flatline refers to asystole, which is the absence of any electrical activity in the heart. In this situation, the heart is not generating any impulses, so there is no rhythm to "reset" or "shock back" into a normal rhythm.

Defibrillation is used to treat certain types of abnormal heart rhythms, specifically ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT), where the heart has chaotic or rapid electrical activity. Defibrillation delivers an electric shock to depolarize the heart muscle and allow the normal pacemaker to re-establish a proper rhythm.

However, in asystole (flatline), defibrillation is not effective because there is no electrical activity to reset. The recommended treatment is high-quality CPR and administration of medications like epinephrine to try to stimulate the heart.

Therefore, defibrillation is not recommended in the case of a cardiac flatline. Instead, CPR is the recommended immediate treatment.

Looking at the options:

A. Yes, defibrillation is used to restart the heart in the case of a cardiac flatline. — Incorrect.

B. Yes, patients can be shocked back to life by a defibrillator in the case of a cardiac flatline. — Incorrect.

C. No, CPR is recommended in the case of a cardiac flatline. — Correct.

D. Yes, defibrillation is recommended in the case of a cardiac flatline. — Incorrect.

E. Yes, defibrillation can return the heart to its regular rhythm in the case of a cardiac flatline. — Incorrect.

Answer: C
